Used carefully, the term names something narrower: the fusion of nation and kingdom into one object of devotion, until you can't find the seam and criticizing the country feels like blasphemy. The mark isn't love of country. It's not being able to tell the difference.

faq.q: Does the study only criticize the political right?
faq.a: No. The version on the right is easier to see because it uses obvious symbols, like a flag on the platform or electoral defeat described as persecution. The study also names a version on the left that fuses the gospel with a progressive movement and reads the prophets as if they wrote for one party. It doesn't claim the two are identical in every respect. It does say each side sees the other's captivity far more easily than its own.

faq.q: What's the difference between patriotism and Christian nationalism?
faq.a: Patriotism is a settled love for a particular place and gratitude for its gifts, and Scripture honors it. Christian nationalism is what happens when that love is asked to admit no limit and fuses with faith until nation and kingdom become one. The test isn't which party you vote for. It's whether, when your country and your Christ point in different directions, you can follow Christ, and whether you can imagine them pointing apart at all.

faq.q: Was Constantine a rescue for the church or a disaster?
faq.a: The study answers: both. The gains were real. The killing stopped, the councils met, and the hospital and a new regard for the weak grew in soil the church could finally tend. But the cost came with the gain. Eusebius saw the emperor as God's chosen instrument, faith became something you could inherit without meeting Christ, and a church protected by the throne found it hard to speak against it. The study names a real gain that carried a captivity inside it.

faq.q: Does "Render to Caesar" teach the separation of church and state?
faq.a: It has been read that way, and that reading has protected real things. Caesar does have a domain; the coin goes back and Jesus leads no tax revolt. But the verse doesn't divide life into two equal drawers. Jesus asks whose likeness is on the coin, using the word Genesis uses for God's image. The coin carries Caesar's image; the person holding it carries God's. Caesar's share is small, and God's is everything.

faq.q: What does the study mean by cultural captivity? Isn't that a way to dismiss people I disagree with?
faq.a: It means the way a church's loves and instincts are shaped by a culture whose influence it never noticed, because the strongest formation is the kind you can't feel. The point is that it applies to the person using the word before anyone else. Captivity rarely feels like captivity; it feels like simply seeing clearly. So the opinion you hold most fiercely, the one that feels least like an opinion, deserves the closest look.

faq.q: Why does the study keep returning to the church under the Nazis and the Barmen Declaration?
faq.a: Because it's the clearest modern case of a church confessing one Lord against a state that demanded a second, and because its best use is as a mirror. In 1934 a movement inside the church was fusing it with the nationalist state and much of the church went along. A minority confessed Christ as the one Word of God, and some, like Bonhoeffer, paid with their lives. The study refuses the easy assumption that we'd have stood with the minority, and asks what second lord we might have added today.

faq.q: Is a free church just a church that stays out of politics?
faq.a: No. Retreat is the quietist's mistake: handing Caesar the public world and keeping God in the private heart. A free church speaks, works for justice, and names the nation's sins as the prophets did. What makes it free is that it does this without giving any earthly power the worship that belongs to God, so that when its Lord and its side part ways, it can follow the Lord.

faq.q: This sounds like an impossible standard. Can any church actually be free?
faq.a: The study doesn't claim to have arrived; it's written toward a free church, not from one. Freedom isn't a place you reach and rest in. It's a refusal made again each day, the same no Jesus said in the wilderness. Certainty about your own side is restful because it asks nothing more of you. Freedom asks you to keep looking. That's harder, but the alternative is a captivity that feels like conviction.

faq.q: I lean strongly one way politically. Will this study just make me uncomfortable?
faq.a: Probably, but not by telling you your convictions don't matter. It asks you to hold them under the lordship of Christ rather than beside it, to apply to your own side the standard you apply to the other, and to extend to the other side the grace you extend to your own. When you try that, you'll likely feel objections rising quickly. That reaction is worth noticing.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't this just the church trying to grab power while pretending to be humble?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study is partly aimed at it. It argues that a church acting as chaplain to a political side is one of the main reasons skeptics won't come near the cross. Rather than defending the church's reach for power, it traces the church's repeated yes to that offer, from Constantine onward, and names it as the very thing Jesus refused. What it asks you to weigh isn't a church taking over the culture but the claim that there is a Lord above every Caesar, made by someone who admits he hasn't escaped the problem himself.

timeline.event: Jesus, after forty days in the wilderness, is shown the kingdoms of the world and offered them for one act of worship. He refuses with Deuteronomy 6:13.
Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus over the tax to Caesar. He asks whose likeness is on the coin.
After the great fire in Rome, Nero blames the Christians and has many put to death, the first large persecution by the Roman state.
Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, writes to the emperor Trajan about the Christians he has executed for refusing to offer incense and wine to the emperor's image and curse Christ.
Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, refuses to call Caesar lord and offer incense, and is burned.
Before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, Constantine reports a sign in the sky with the words "by this sign conquer," and wins.
Constantine and Licinius agree the policy known as the Edict of Milan, ending the persecution of Christians.
The Council of Nicaea meets, called by Constantine.
Under Theodosius, Nicene Christianity becomes the official religion of the empire.
Ambrose of Milan requires Theodosius to do public penance for the massacre at Thessalonica.
Rome is sacked. Pagans blame the Christians, and Augustine begins to answer them.
Augustine writes the City of God, refusing to identify the kingdom of God with any earthly regime.
As a movement inside the church works to fuse it with the Nazi state, a minority meets at Barmen and confesses Jesus Christ as the one Word of God.
Bonhoeffer publishes Discipleship, naming cheap grace.
Bonhoeffer is hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April, weeks before the war in Europe ends.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thanks for being here. This may be one of the hardest subjects a church can talk about together, so let me say three things before we start. First, this isn't a political study, and I'm not going to tell anyone how to vote. It's about the cross and who the church belongs to, and it holds every side to the same Lord. Second, this is a safe room. You can have a strong conviction questioned here without being treated as a fool, and you can sit next to someone who votes differently without this turning into a debate. Third, I'm in this too. I'll name my own side's blind spots before I ask you to look at anyone else's. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a minute before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into our own loyalties, the convictions we hold so tightly they don't feel like opinions anymore. And remember, we start with our own house, not the other side's.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop here, even though it isn't tied up, because this subject doesn't resolve into a tidy political conclusion. The offer is still on the mountain, and so is the cross. Take this toward Christ this week rather than back into your side's arguments. Try the practice, and spend some time with the reflection questions, especially the ones that turn toward you. If tonight showed you something in your own heart you hadn't seen, don't rush to defend it. Let me pray for us before we go.

bibliography.title: Discipleship (The Cost of Discipleship)
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Published in German in 1937. The source of the idea of cheap grace. Central to session 5.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Written 413 to 426, after the sack of Rome. Distinguishes the city of God from the earthly city. Central to session 3.

bibliography.title: The Theological Declaration of Barmen (1934)
bibliography.author: Karl Barth and others, for the Confessing Synod at Barmen
bibliography.note: Short, and worth reading whole. Its first article confesses Jesus Christ as the one Word of God. Central to session 5.

bibliography.title: The Myth of Religious Violence
bibliography.author: William T. Cavanaugh
bibliography.note: 2009. Questions the story that the secular state ended religious violence as a neutral referee. Background for session 4.

bibliography.title: Taking America Back for God: Christian Nationalism in the United States
bibliography.author: Andrew L. Whitehead and Samuel L. Perry
bibliography.note: 2020. A sociological attempt to define and measure Christian nationalism as distinct from ordinary religion and patriotism. Useful for session 2.

bibliography.title: Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas and William H. Willimon
bibliography.note: 1989. Argues the church is a colony of resident aliens rather than a chaplain to the culture.

bibliography.title: The Gospel in a Pluralist Society
bibliography.author: Lesslie Newbigin
bibliography.note: 1989. Treats the West as a mission field and the end of Christendom as a chance to recover the church as a witness.

bibliography.title: Desiring the Kingdom
bibliography.author: James K. A. Smith
bibliography.note: 2009. On how we're formed by what we love and repeat, and how a culture shapes us through practices we never chose. Background for the idea of cultural captivity.

bibliography.title: A Secular Age
bibliography.author: Charles Taylor
bibliography.note: 2007. Traces how the modern West came to live within what Taylor calls the immanent frame, a way of seeing we were trained into more than reasoned into.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: About 397 to 400. Augustine's account of disordered loves, which underlies the study's language about divided loyalties.

bibliography.title: The Benedict Option
bibliography.author: Rod Dreher
bibliography.note: 2017. One contested answer to the end of Christendom, arguing for a more deliberate withdrawal into strong communities. Offered for a group to weigh against this study's call to engaged witness, not as the study's position.

furtherReading: Discipleship, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for those who want to sit longer with cheap grace and costly following.
The Theological Declaration of Barmen, read whole, for the six confessions and rejections behind session 5.
Resident Aliens, Stanley Hauerwas and William H. Willimon, for a picture of the church as a colony rather than a chaplain.
The Gospel in a Pluralist Society, Lesslie Newbigin, for readers grieving the end of Christendom who want to see what it might make possible.
Desiring the Kingdom, James K. A. Smith, for those who want to think about how culture shapes our loves without our noticing.

glossary.definition: The devil's offer of all the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship, refused by Jesus (Matthew 4:8-10). The study treats it as the pattern for every later temptation to reach the kingdom's ends by the world's means.
Not love of country, but the fusion of two loyalties into one, so that nation and kingdom become a single object of devotion. Its mark is the inability to tell the difference.

The welding of faith and a nation or political movement until the seam disappears and criticizing one feels like betraying the other. It can happen on the left or the right, and the gospel is always what gets bent.
The arrangement, beginning under Constantine, in which belonging to the culture and belonging to the church became the same thing.
Someone whose faith is mostly belonging to a civilization, inherited like a family name, without ever having met Christ in it.
The condition of a church shaped in its loves and instincts by a culture whose influence it never noticed. Captivity rarely feels like captivity; it feels like seeing clearly.
Jesus' answer to a trap about taxes (Mark 12:17). It doesn't divide life into two equal drawers; it asks what carries God's image, and the answer is the person holding the coin.

The likeness God gave humanity at creation (Genesis 1:27). The Greek word is the same one used of Caesar's likeness on the coin. Because the person bears God's image, no part of a person belongs to the state.
Blending faith in God with a second devotion until the worshiper can't tell that two are being served. Israel rarely abandoned the Lord outright; it more often added another loyalty.

In the Old Testament, a local shrine where Israel worshiped the Lord alongside other gods, left standing through reform after reform because it felt like the way things had always been. Used here for any second devotion that arrived without anyone deciding it should.
Bonhoeffer's term, in Discipleship (1937), for grace that asks for no repentance and no following, and so can be fitted to almost anything.
The Barmen Declaration's confession (1934) that Jesus Christ, as attested in Scripture, is the one Word of God to be heard, trusted, and obeyed, with no second source beside him.
A chaplain blesses what we've already decided. A Lord can command, redirect, and call us to repent. The captive church wants a chaplain and calls him Lord.

Not a church that has withdrawn from public life, but one that engages without fusing, refusing to give any earthly power the worship that belongs to God, so it can follow Christ when he and its side part ways.
